paras: The St. Louis Broadway streetcar shooting took place at about 1:30 a.m. on 16 August 1905, when a group of young men harassed Clarence (or Charles) Hunt, a Black youth, on a streetcar near Broadway and Olive street in St. Louis, Missouri, and one of them fired a revolver at him. The shots missed Hunt but wounded two other passengers, Sam Edwards, a Black man, and John Rogers. Beverly Brown, whom Edwards and Hunt identified as the gunman, was arrested and denied the charge.

According to the St. Louis Republic, a "gang of young fellows" boarded the crowded car at Broadway, and one of them pulled the sleeping Hunt into the aisle by his legs. Hunt later said the trouble began when Brown ordered him out of his seat and called him a "nigger." After passengers intervened, the men got off, one remarking, "He's only a nigger, anyhow," and a man then fired through the car at Hunt. Rogers and Edwards, passengers "who had no part in the controversy," were hit in the legs, and police arrested one of the fleeing men, Thomas Lamb, a self-described former police officer.

Later that day detectives arrested Brown at the Pickwick Club, in which he and Lamb were said to have an interest; Brown was held for investigation and Lamb, now called Townley, as an accessory. No warrant was to be issued until Rogers identified the prisoners, and no later report of a charge or trial appears in the coverage.

Only the St. Louis Republic covered the shooting, first on page 1 under "TWO SHOT WHILE ON STREET CAR," with the deck "Shots Fired at Negro, on Broadway and Olive, Strike Passengers in Legs." The story quoted the slur and stressed that the wounded were bystanders. Its page-5 follow-up, "ACCUSED OF SHOOTING TWO MEN ON BROADWAY CAR," set the two Black witnesses' identification of Brown beside his denial. No Black-press coverage was found.
The first report called the wounds slight, while the second said Edwards had "a severe wound in the hip" and that Rogers was more seriously hurt.

reader.title: St. Louis Broadway streetcar shooting
bases: A group of young white men pulled a Black youth from his seat on a streetcar, and one of them fired at him, wounding two other passengers; no one was killed (A1, A2).
Both reports of the shooting come from one paper, the St. Louis Republic (A1, A2); they agree on the core event, but no independent paper or Black-press account was found.

1 (Edwards); Rogers was also wounded, race not stated.

record_check.record: On a Broadway streetcar in St. Louis, Beverly Brown ordered Charles Hunt, a Black passenger, out of his seat, called him a 'nigger', and is accused of shooting Samuel Edwards, a Black man, and John Rogers.
record_check.dossier: That Brown ordered Hunt from his seat and used the slur is Hunt's account; the first report describes a gang dragging Hunt into the aisle and one man firing at him, the shots hitting Edwards and Rogers.
single_source: two reports, both in the St. Louis Republic.

info: About 1:30 a.m., 16 August 1905 ('1:30 this morning' in the 16 August paper; 'early yesterday morning' on 17 August)
On a streetcar as it neared Broadway at Olive street, St. Louis; called an 'Olive street car' (A1) and a 'Broadway car at Olive street' (A2)

Target: Clarence (A1) or Charles (A2) Hunt, described as 'a negro boy'; wounded: Sam (Samuel) Edwards, 'a negro', and John Rogers, whose race is not stated, both described as passengers with no part in the quarrel
'A gang of young fellows' who boarded at Broadway; one fired a revolver. Beverly Brown was accused of the shooting and Townley (or Thomas) Lamb was held as an accessory
Unknown. No later report of the shooting case was found; on 13 September Brown's separate liquor-license case was dismissed
